details: In a text, `[iberian_struggle|E]` shows "Iberian Struggle" linked to the concept's explanation. The struggle moves between phases of violence, wary truce and practical cooperation, and the description warns that a shared faith or culture is no guarantee of alliance.

summary: Another name of the game concept Artifact Rarity: how rare an artifact is.
details: In a text, `[illustrious|E]` shows the word "Illustrious" linked to the Artifact Rarity explanation. Illustrious is the highest rarity level, above masterwork and famed; common is the lowest and never shown.

label: Expedite schemes decision
summary: The game concept Expedite Schemes Decision: a decision that speeds up your schemes.
details: In a text, `[impatient_rushing_all_schemes_decision|E]` shows "Expedite Schemes Decision" linked to the concept's explanation. The decision gives scheme opportunities in exchange for stress.

label: Imperial family
summary: Another name of the game concept Imperial Family: the top house in a bureaucratic realm.
details: In a text, `[imperial|E]` shows the word "Imperial" linked to the Imperial Family explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Imperial bureaucracy
summary: The game concept Imperial Bureaucracy: how centralized an administrative realm is and how much power its ruler has over vassals.
details: In a text, `[imperial_bureaucracy|E]` shows "Imperial Bureaucracy" linked to the concept's explanation. Only the top liege can change it, and administrative vassals use their liege's level. It has four levels.

label: Civil service examination
summary: The game concept Civil Service Examination: the exams through which bureaucrats of celestial and meritocratic governments are chosen by merit.
details: In a text, `[imperial_examination|E]` shows "Civil Service Examination" linked to the concept's explanation. Through the exams, able scholars of any background can gain governorships. The exams have several levels.

label: Civil service examination
summary: Another name of the game concept Civil Service Examination: the exams through which bureaucrats are chosen by merit.
details: In a text, `[imperial_examinations|E]` shows the plural "Civil Service Examinations" linked to the concept's explanation.

label: Imperial expedition
summary: The game concept Imperial Expedition: a very strong reason for war that co-emperors in a duumvirate can use.
details: In a text, `[imperial_expedition_cb|E]` shows "Imperial Expedition" linked to the concept's explanation. It can target any realm that borders the empire or holds land that de jure belongs to the senior emperor, and usually takes all duchies that border the empire or belong to it. Every governor bordering the defender is forced into the war.

label: Imperial expedition
summary: Another name of the game concept Imperial Expedition: a very strong reason for war that co-emperors in a duumvirate can use.
details: In a text, `[imperial_expedition_cb_expedition|E]` shows just the word "Expedition" linked to the Imperial Expedition explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Imperial grace
summary: The game concept Imperial Grace: the standing the Son of Heaven grants a tributary.
details: In a text, `[imperial_grace|E]` shows "Imperial Grace" linked to the concept's explanation. High grace can bring the tributary special privileges during tribute missions. At low grace the Son of Heaven may demand tribute, and at zero the relationship can end.

label: Imperial policy
summary: Another name of the game concept Imperial Policy: a law that the top liege of Japan sets for all vassals.
details: In a text, `[imperial_policies|E]` shows the plural "Imperial Policies" linked to the Imperial Policy explanation.

label: Imperial policy
summary: The game concept Imperial Policy: a law that the top liege of Japan sets and that applies to all vassals.
details: In a text, `[imperial_policy|E]` shows "Imperial Policy" linked to the concept's explanation. A policy can forbid or allow actions, or give effects across the whole realm.

label: Imperial policy faction
summary: The game concept Imperial Policy Faction: a faction that wants to change the realm's imperial policy to a new law its leader picks.
details: In a text, `[imperial_policy_faction|E]` shows the faction's name ("... Faction") linked to the concept's explanation.

label: Imperial policy faction
summary: Another name of the game concept Imperial Policy Faction: a faction that wants to change the realm's imperial policy.
details: In a text, `[imperial_policy_factions|E]` shows the plural "Imperial Policy Factions" linked to the Imperial Policy Faction explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Treasury
summary: Another name of the game concept Treasury: under certain governments, funds that can only be spent on government purposes, apart from personal gold.
details: In a text, `[imperial_treasury|E]` shows "Imperial Treasury" linked to the Treasury explanation. The treasury is built up either by the top liege (centralized) or locally (decentralized), and part of tax income goes into it; a vassal may receive treasury from their liege based on their tax contributions.

label: Implicit claim
summary: The game concept Implicit Claim: a claim that eligible children get on every title their parents hold.
details: In a text, `[implicit_claim|E]` shows "Implicit Claim" linked to the concept's explanation. If the parent loses the title, the child's implicit claim on it goes too.

details: In a text, `[imprison|E]` shows the word "Imprison" linked to the Prison explanation. Characters can be imprisoned after battles and sieges, and rulers can arrest anyone in their realm, though that counts as tyranny unless the character is guilty of a crime.

details: In a text, `[inbred|E]` shows the word "Inbred" linked to the Inbreeding explanation.

label: Inbreeding
summary: The game concept Inbreeding: the risk that the children of two close relatives are born with a congenital defect.
details: In a text, `[inbreeding|E]` shows "Inbreeding" linked to the concept's explanation. The worst defect is the Inbred trait. The risk is low in the first generation and grows with each further one; inbreeding can also produce the helpful Pure-blooded trait.

label: Incest
summary: The game concept Incest: sexual relations between close relatives.
details: In a text, `[incest|E]` shows "Incest" linked to the concept's explanation. Which relations count as incest depends on the consanguinity doctrine of the character's faith. No vanilla text uses this name; vanilla writes `[incestuous|E]`.

label: Foment revolt

details: In a text, `[incite_revolts_interaction|E]` shows "Foment Revolt" linked to the concept's explanation. It needs counties there with negative county opinion.

label: Income
summary: The game concept Income: the gold a character earns.
details: In a text, `[income|E]` shows "Income" linked to the concept's explanation. Its two main sources are taxes from your own holdings and from your vassals.

label: Increase control in county
summary: The game concept Increase Control in County: a council task of the marshal that raises control in a county.
details: In a text, `[increase_control|E]` shows "Increase Control in County" linked to the concept's explanation. The task targets one county, raises its control and removes county corruption over time.

label: Independence faction
summary: The game concept Independence Faction: a faction that wants independence for all its members.
details: In a text, `[independence_faction|E]` shows "Independence Faction" linked to the concept's explanation. If it succeeds, its members break free of their liege.

details: In a text, `[independence_factions|E]` shows the plural "Independence Factions" linked to the Independence Faction explanation.

label: Independent ruler
summary: Another name of the game concept Independent Ruler: a ruler without a liege.
details: In a text, `[independent|E]` shows the word "Independent" linked to the Independent Ruler explanation. Independent rulers have more freedom, for example in declaring wars, but unlike vassals they can be attacked directly by foreign rulers.

label: Independent ruler

details: In a text, `[independent_ruler|E]` shows "Independent Ruler" linked to the concept's explanation. Such rulers have more freedom, for example in declaring wars, but unlike vassals they can be attacked directly by foreign rulers.

details: In a text, `[independent_rulers|E]` shows the plural "Independent Rulers" linked to the Independent Ruler explanation.

label: Chance of infection

details: In a text, `[infection_chance|E]` shows "Chance of Infection" linked to the concept's explanation.

label: Infection rate
summary: The game concept Infection Rate: how severe an epidemic is in an affected barony and how strong its effects are there.
details: In a text, `[infection_rate|E]` shows "Infection Rate" linked to the concept's explanation. Left alone, the rate always climbs towards its maximum; minor, major and apocalyptic epidemics climb at different speeds. Rulers can soften it by raising their realm's epidemic resistance.

label: Infection rate
summary: Another name of the game concept Infection Rate: how severe an epidemic is in an affected barony.
details: In a text, `[infection_rates|E]` shows the plural "Infection Rates" linked to the Infection Rate explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Mitigate infirmity

details: In a text, `[infirm_mitigation|E]` shows "Mitigate Infirmity" linked to the concept's explanation. The Infirm trait gains a full level with each illness and a little every year; it advances much faster during long sickness and after age 65. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Influence
summary: The game concept Influence: a character's political reach and authority in a realm with administrative government.
details: In a text, `[influence|E]` shows "Influence" linked to the concept's explanation. It is gained in many ways, such as being a governor, upgrading an estate, or being allied to the house head of a noble family. Its main use is acquiring a governorship. Vanilla uses it very widely.

label: Influence
summary: Another name of the game concept Influence: a character's political reach in a realm with administrative government.
details: In a text, `[influence_i|E]` shows the influence icon (not a word) linked to the Influence explanation. Vanilla often puts it before influence amounts.

details: In a text, `[influence_level|E]` shows "Level of Influence" linked to the concept's explanation. Every gain of influence also brings progress towards the next level, and each level gives its own modifiers.

label: Level of influence impact

details: In a text, `[influence_level_impact|E]` shows "Level of Influence Impact" linked to the concept's explanation.

details: In a text, `[influential|E]` shows the word "Influential" linked to the Influence explanation.

label: Initial legitimacy
summary: The game concept Initial Legitimacy: the legitimacy a character starts with when they become landed.
details: In a text, `[initial_legitimacy|E]` shows "Initial Legitimacy" linked to the concept's explanation. It is worked out from many things, among them dynasty prestige level, relation to the predecessor, court grandeur, gender, bastardy, years as a ruler, diplomacy, virtues, sins and some special traits.

label: Innovation
summary: The game concept Innovation: a technology or other advance that benefits every character of a culture.
details: In a text, `[innovation|E]` shows "Innovation" linked to the concept's explanation. Innovations are grouped by the era in which they can be discovered. Contact with neighboring cultures always spreads one innovation to a culture, which it then discovers much faster, and the culture head can set a cultural fascination for an extra boost.

label: Innovation
summary: Another name of the game concept Innovation: a technology or other advance that benefits every character of a culture.
details: In a text, `[innovations|E]` shows the plural "Innovations" linked to the Innovation explanation.

label: Inspection

details: In a text, `[inspection|E]` shows "Inspection" linked to the concept's explanation. The inspection brings opportunities in one chosen focus area.

details: In a text, `[inspection_i|E]` shows the inspection activity icon (not a word) linked to the Inspection explanation.

label: Inspection success chance
summary: The game concept Inspection Success Chance: how likely an inspection is to succeed.
details: The game names learning, county control and a bordering foreign realm as the main factors, and the chance never goes above 95%. In a text, `[inspection_success_chance|E]` shows the words linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in the modifiers for a second, third and fourth try at an inspection (+10%, +20%, +30%).

label: Inspection success chance
summary: Another name of the game concept Inspection Success Chance, shown as just "Success Chance".
details: In a text, `[inspection_success_chance_no_prefix|E]` shows the shorter words linked to the same explanation; vanilla uses it where the sentence already makes clear it is about an inspection, as in "Improves the Success Chance". The chance depends mainly on learning, county control and a bordering foreign realm, and is at most 95%.

label: Inspection

details: In a text, `[inspections|E]` shows the word "Inspections" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in the survey activity's texts, for example that inspections cannot be held in the capital and only once every 5 years in a county.

label: Inspiration
summary: The game concept Inspiration: a skilled artisan's project that can come true if someone sponsors it.
details: An inspired character can be hired, for example through the Commission Artifact decision, and when the project is done the sponsor keeps the result, normally an artifact. In a text, `[inspiration|E]` shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in court amenity texts about the quality of completed inspirations.

label: Inspiration
summary: The plural name of the game concept Inspiration: skilled artisans' projects that come true when someone sponsors them.
details: In a text, `[inspirations|E]` shows the word "Inspirations" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in building effects such as "Increased Quality of Sponsored inspirations".

details: The sponsor keeps the finished result, normally an artifact. In a text, `[inspired|E]` shows the word linked to the inspiration explanation. Vanilla uses it for characters who may become inspired, in court position and court type texts.

label: Integrate title
summary: The game concept Integrate Title: a council task of the chancellor that speeds up a title's de jure drift.
details: De jure drift is the game's process by which a title shifts to become lawfully part of another one; at full progress this task makes the target title de jure part of the ruler's primary title. The word shown is the task's own name, "Integrate Title". In a text, `[integrate_title|E]` shows it linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in decision and modifier texts that give a bonus to this task when it targets a certain county.

label: Intent
summary: The game concept Intent: what a character personally wants to achieve at an activity.
details: The host and every guest each have their own intent. In a text, `[intent|E]` shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it after the name of a specific intent, in achievement and effect texts ("Can use the Seduce intent freely").

label: Intent
summary: The plural name of the game concept Intent: what the characters at an activity each want to achieve there.
details: In a text, `[intents|E]` shows the word "Intents" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in the activity window's conclusion ("Succeeded intents") and in the coronation's explanation of magnificence.

label: Interaction
summary: Another name of the game concept Interaction, shown as "Interacting": actions one character takes towards another.
details: In a text, `[interacting|E]` shows the word linked to the interaction explanation. Vanilla uses it in the powerful family texts: such families are more likely to get what they want when interacting with other characters.

label: Interaction
summary: The game concept Interaction: an action one character takes towards another, usually picked from the menu when right-clicking a character.
details: Interactions serve many purposes; some need the target's approval and some do not, and a few are reached through special windows. In a text, `[interaction|E]` shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it often (about 300 uses), mostly after the name of a specific interaction, as in "Unlocks the ... interaction".

label: Interaction
summary: The plural name of the game concept Interaction: actions one character takes towards another.
details: In a text, `[interactions|E]` shows the word "Interactions" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in effect texts after naming several interactions, such as a bonus to their acceptance.

label: Internal upgrade
summary: Another name of the game concept Internal Upgrade, in the plural: an improvement that can only be built inside one specific domicile building.
details: Domicile buildings are the buildings of a domicile (a character's own seat, such as a yurt); each building that allows upgrades has its own set. In a text, `[internal_upgrades|E]` shows "Internal Upgrades" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in domicile and yurt texts.

label: Intimidated
summary: The game concept Intimidated: a character who greatly fears another character.
details: The fear usually comes from dread and a cowardly personality. Intimidated characters are less likely to act against the one they fear, for example to join or start factions; characters who are even more afraid are cowed. In a text, `[intimidated|E]` shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in faction reasons, decisions and interaction acceptance texts.

label: Intimidated
summary: The icon form of the game concept Intimidated (a character who greatly fears another).
details: `[intimidated_i]` shows the intimidated icon (`@intimidated_icon!`) instead of a word. Vanilla puts it right before `[intimidated|E]`, as in "You are intimidated by them".

label: Intimidation tour
summary: The game concept Intimidation Tour: a kind of tour on which the ruler tries to frighten their vassals.
details: It gains the ruler dread and forces vassals out of factions. The other tour types named by the game are the majesty and taxation tours. In a text, `[intimidation_tour|E]` shows the words linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in an achievement and in the explanation of tour types.

label: Intrigue
summary: Another name of the game concept Intrigue Skill, shown as "Intrigue": the skill for understanding and manipulating others and organizing plots.
details: It mainly helps to run intrigue schemes and to defend against them; its lifestyle is the intrigue lifestyle. In a text, `[intrigue|E]` shows the word linked to the skill's explanation. Vanilla uses it often (over 200 uses), for example as the name of the intrigue modifier and in board game events.

label: Intrigue (number code)
summary: A coded name of the Intrigue Lifestyle game concept: the word INTRIGUE as letter numbers.
details: The game lists it as an alias of the intrigue_lifestyle concept, shown as "9 14 20 18 9 7 21 5" (the alphabet positions of INTRIGUE). `[intrigue_9_14_20_18_9_7_21_5|E]` in a text shows that code linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in an intrigue scheming event: "You gain ... [coded] points".

label: Intrigue
summary: The icon form of the game concept Intrigue Skill (the skill for manipulating others and plotting).
details: `[intrigue_i]` shows the intrigue skill icon (`@skill_intrigue_icon!`) instead of a word. Vanilla puts it right before `[intrigue|E]` or `[intrigue_skill|E]`, for example in the spymaster's council task texts.

label: Intrigue lifestyle
summary: The game concept Intrigue Lifestyle: the lifestyle for characters who want to succeed in schemes, gain dread or seduce others easily.
details: In a text, `[intrigue_lifestyle|E]` shows the words linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in effect texts about gaining intrigue lifestyle experience.

label: Intrigue lifestyle icon
summary: The Intrigue Lifestyle game concept, shown as its icon.
details: The game lists it as an alias of the intrigue_lifestyle concept, and its text is the intrigue lifestyle icon. Vanilla puts `[intrigue_lifestyle_i]` at the start of a bookmark character's description.

label: Intrigue (letter code)
summary: A coded name of the Intrigue Lifestyle game concept: the word intrigue with each letter shifted three places.
details: The game lists it as an alias of the intrigue_lifestyle concept, shown as "Lqwuljxh". `[intrigue_lqwuljxh|E]` in a text shows that word linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in an intrigue scheming event: "You gain ... [coded] points".

label: Intrigue lifestyle
summary: Another name of the game concept Intrigue Lifestyle, shown as the unusual word "Rigueint".
details: The game's concept file lists it as an alias of the intrigue lifestyle, and its text is "Rigueint". In a text, `[intrigue_rigueint|E]` shows that word linked to the intrigue lifestyle's explanation. Vanilla uses it once, in an intrigue scheming event ("You gain ... points").

label: Intrigue skill
summary: The game concept Intrigue Skill: the skill for understanding and manipulating other characters and organizing plots.
details: It mainly helps to run intrigue schemes and to defend against them; its lifestyle is the intrigue lifestyle. In a text, `[intrigue_skill|E]` shows the words linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in interaction, court position and succession law texts.

label: Intrigue contract
summary: The game concept Intrigue Contract: a task contract, typically about anything from scouting to breaking someone out of prison.
details: In a text, `[intrigue_task_contract|E]` shows "Intrigue Contract" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Intrigue contract's
summary: The possessive form of the game concept Intrigue Contract (a task contract about scouting, jailbreaks and the like).
details: In a text, `[intrigue_task_contract_possessive|E]` shows "Intrigue Contract's" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Intrigue contract
summary: The plural name of the game concept Intrigue Contract: task contracts about anything from scouting to jailbreaks.
details: In a text, `[intrigue_task_contracts|E]` shows "Intrigue Contracts" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it once, in a decision event that creates such contracts on the map.

label: Intrigue contracts'
summary: The plural possessive form of the game concept Intrigue Contract (task contracts about scouting, jailbreaks and the like).
details: In a text, `[intrigue_task_contracts_possessive|E]` shows "Intrigue Contracts'" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Inventory artifact
summary: The game concept Inventory Artifact: an artifact a character wears or carries, such as a weapon or a crown.
details: A character can own any number of them, but only those equipped in a slot of their kind have an effect. New ones come from inspired characters or the Commission Artifact decision. In a text, `[inventory_artifact|E]` shows the words linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in artifact texts such as "Must be a child to equip as an inventory artifact".

label: Inventory artifact
summary: The plural name of the game concept Inventory Artifact: artifacts a character wears or carries.
details: In a text, `[inventory_artifacts|E]` shows "Inventory Artifacts" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in the artifact explanations, next to court artifacts, which stay in a ruler's royal court instead.

label: Investment capacity
summary: The game concept Investment Capacity: the most a character can invest in their own or someone else's candidate score for a title.
details: For governorships the main factors are age, powerful family rating, influence level and estate buildings; for clerical appointments, age and piety level. Children get a small penalty, and an adult's limit rises with age. In a text, `[investment_cap|E]` shows "Investment Capacity" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in house bonuses and in a warning that a contribution is smaller once the cap is reached.

label: Jailor
summary: Another name of the game concept Prison, shown as "Jailor": rulers keeping other characters as prisoners.
details: Prisoners are kept in a dungeon or under house arrest (in a camp, in the stockade) and can be executed, tortured or ransomed, among other things; arresting someone who committed no crime is seen as tyrannical. In a text, `[jailor|E]` shows the word linked to the prison explanation. The vanilla lines given, like `[jailor.GetTitledFirstName]`, are a different thing: they use a saved character named `jailor`, not this concept.

label: Ritsuryō government
summary: Another name of the game concept Ritsuryō Government, shown as "Ritsuryō": the centralized, bureaucratic government unique to Japan.
details: Under it, characters are appointed as governors for their liege and use influence, and the heads of noble families have a family manor and a house aspiration; a kampaku governs on behalf of the Japanese emperor. In a text, `[japan_administrative|E]` shows the word linked to the government's explanation. Vanilla uses it before `[government|E]`, for example in a character list filter and a modifier name.

label: Sōryō government
summary: Another name of the game concept Sōryō Government, shown as "Sōryō": the feudal government unique to Japan.
details: It stands for local lords who pushed aside the central ritsuryō government and rule provinces as their own fiefs. They do not use influence, but noble family heads keep their family manor and house aspiration. In a text, `[japan_feudal|E]` shows the word linked to the government's explanation. Vanilla lists it with other feudal-like governments in succession law and tradition texts.

label: Japanese bureaucracy
summary: The game concept Japanese Bureaucracy: how centralized a Ritsuryō realm is and how much power its ruler has over the vassals.
details: Only the top liege can change it, and Japanese vassals use their liege's level; there are four levels. In a text, `[japanese_bureaucracy|E]` shows the words linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it as the government's authority law ("Use Japanese Bureaucracy as government authority").

label: Japanese emperor
summary: The game concept Japanese Emperor: the official emperor (Ten'nō) of all Japan.
details: Real power usually lies with the ceremonial regent, who runs the state on the emperor's behalf. In a text, `[japanese_emperor|E]` shows the words linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in the Japanese government texts, for example that a kampaku governs on behalf of the emperor.

label: Japanese emperor's
summary: The possessive form of the game concept Japanese Emperor (the official emperor of all Japan).
details: In a text, `[japanese_emperor_possessive|E]` shows "Japanese Emperor's" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it once, in a Japanese career event ("the Japanese Emperor's subjects").

label: Japanese manor
summary: The game concept Japanese Manor: a domicile held by the head of a notable noble family in a Ritsuryō or Sōryō realm.
details: It stands for private land that is not tied to any landed title, and manor buildings can be built there to grow the family's wealth and influence. In a text, `[japanese_manor|E]` shows the words linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in house aspiration and manor building texts.

label: Japanese manor building
summary: The game concept Japanese Manor Building: a lasting improvement the owner builds in a Japanese manor.
details: There are many kinds; they can bring private income, more influence for the family, and access to decisions, interactions and more. In a text, `[japanese_manor_building|E]` shows the words linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in the manor's explanation and in a modifier that lowers the cost of a tea manor building by 25%.

label: Japanese manor building
summary: The plural name of the game concept Japanese Manor Building: lasting improvements built in a Japanese manor.
details: In a text, `[japanese_manor_buildings|E]` shows "Japanese Manor Buildings" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this name in a link.

label: Japanese manor
summary: The plural name of the game concept Japanese Manor: domiciles of the heads of notable Japanese noble families.
details: In a text, `[japanese_manors|E]` shows "Japanese Manors" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Jihad
summary: Another name of the game concept Directed Great Holy War, shown as "Jihad": a great holy war that a temporal head of faith declares to take a kingdom for themselves.
details: Rulers of the same faith may join in and can be rewarded with piety, and possibly with their dynasty getting land in the conquered kingdom; rulers of the target religion may defend. In a text, `[jihad|E]` shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Jihad
summary: The plural of another name of the game concept Directed Great Holy War, shown as "Jihads": great holy wars a temporal head of faith declares to take a kingdom.
details: In a text, `[jihads|E]` shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Jōkō
summary: Another name of the game concept Cloistered Emperor, shown as "Jōkō": a retired Japanese emperor who rules in practice as ceremonial regent for the reigning emperor.
details: To become one, an emperor must give up the Chrysanthemum Throne and become a monk. In a text, `[joko|E]` shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it once, in a faction text: only a kampaku or jōkō can be replaced.

label: Jōkō's
summary: The possessive form of Jōkō, another name of the game concept Cloistered Emperor (a retired Japanese emperor who still rules in practice).
details: In a text, `[joko_possessive|E]` shows "Jōkō's" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Nominal co-emperor
summary: Another name of the game concept Nominal Duumvirate, shown as "Nominal Co-Emperor": the junior of two emperors who share one empire.
details: A duumvirate is one empire ruled by a senior emperor (the liege) and a junior emperor. It is nominal while the junior emperor is a child, and becomes a full duumvirate when they grow up; junior emperors give passive influence to themselves and the senior emperor. In a text, `[junior_emperor|E]` shows the words linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in faction reasons and in the explanation of time in office.

label: Nominal co-emperor
summary: The plural of another name of the game concept Nominal Duumvirate, shown as "Nominal Co-Emperors": junior emperors who share an empire with a senior one.
details: In a text, `[junior_emperors|E]` shows the words linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Justicar contract
summary: The game concept Justicar Contract: a task contract, typically about hunting down criminals while bringing justice and keeping to local law.
details: In a text, `[justicar_task_contract|E]` shows "Justicar Contract" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Justicar contract's
summary: The possessive form of the game concept Justicar Contract (a task contract about hunting down criminals).
details: In a text, `[justicar_task_contract_possessive|E]` shows "Justicar Contract's" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Justicar contract
summary: The plural name of the game concept Justicar Contract: task contracts about hunting down criminals under local law.
details: In a text, `[justicar_task_contracts|E]` shows "Justicar Contracts" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in decisions that create such contracts on the map ("Creates up to 3 ...").

label: Justicar contracts'
summary: The plural possessive form of the game concept Justicar Contract (task contracts about hunting down criminals).
details: In a text, `[justicar_task_contracts_possessive|E]` shows "Justicar Contracts'" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Kampaku
summary: The game concept Kampaku: in practice the highest office of the Ritsuryō bureaucracy, running the state in the emperor's place.
details: The Fujiwara family usually holds it, but any family with enough influence and prestige can rise to it. In a text, `[kampaku|E]` shows the word linked to the concept's explanation, as in "Only a kampaku or jōkō can be replaced". Vanilla lines like `[kampaku.GetName]` are a different thing: they use a saved character named `kampaku`, not this concept.

label: Kampaku's
summary: The possessive form of the game concept Kampaku (the highest office of the Ritsuryō bureaucracy in practice).
details: In a text, `[kampaku_possessive|E]` shows "Kampaku's" linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: Kindle royal fire decision
summary: The game concept Kindle Royal Fire Decision: a decision to light a royal fire, which gives bonuses to health and dynasty prestige.
details: In a text, `[kindle_royal_fire_decision|E]` shows the words linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this name.

label: King
summary: The game concept King: a ruler whose primary title is a kingdom.
details: Kings rank above dukes and below emperors, so they can have dukes and lower rulers as vassals, and an emperor as liege. In a text, `[king|E]` shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in elective succession reasons and other concept explanations.

label: Kingdom
summary: The game concept Kingdom: a title one tier below an empire and one above a duchy.
details: Its holder has de jure (lawful) rights to the land it is made of. A kingdom can be dormant with no holder; then a ruler who controls at least half of its counties can create it. In a text, `[kingdom|E]` shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it often (about 240 uses), for example in achievements.

label: Kingdom
summary: The plural name of the game concept Kingdom: titles one tier below an empire and one above a duchy.
details: In a text, `[kingdoms|E]` shows "Kingdoms" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in decisions that make kingdoms de jure part of a new empire.

label: King
summary: The plural name of the game concept King: rulers whose primary title is a kingdom.
details: In a text, `[kings|E]` shows "Kings" linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in faction reasons ("Kings desire independence") and in other rank explanations.

label: Kinslayer
summary: Another name of the game concept Kinslaying, shown as "Kinslayer": a character known to have killed a family member.
details: Some faiths treat it as a crime. There are three kinslayer traits, by how close the victim was: close family, extended family, or another member of the dynasty. In a text, `[kinslayer|E]` shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in elective succession and papal election reasons.

label: Kinslayer
summary: The plural of another name of the game concept Kinslaying, shown as "Kinslayers": characters known to have killed a family member.
details: In a text, `[kinslayers|E]` shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. Vanilla uses it in faith doctrine texts about which kinslayers count as criminals.

label: Kinslaying
summary: The game concept Kinslaying: killing a member of one's own family.
details: Some faiths treat it as a crime, and there are three kinslayer traits by how close the victim was (close family, extended family, other dynasty members). In a text, `[kinslaying|E]` shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. No vanilla text uses this exact name in a link.

label: Knight
summary: The game concept Knight: a vassal, courtier or follower who fights in person in your army.
details: In battle, knights use their prowess: high prowess means more damage to the enemy and a better chance to survive unharmed. In a text, `[knight|E]` shows the word linked to the concept's explanation. Many vanilla lines like `[knight.GetFullName]` are a different thing: they use a saved character named `knight`, not this concept.
